perf.summary: The per-rule `int* rhs = stackalloc int[rhsLen]` inside the while loop stack-allocates repeatedly in a loop.
perf.currentCost: stackalloc inside a loop body: in C# the stack space is not freed until method return, so each iteration grows the frame — effectively unbounded stack growth proportional to number of expansions, risking stack overflow and defeating the bounded-frame assumption. The rhs copy is also redundant.
perf.proposedChange: Eliminate the rhs temporary entirely: push directly from the table in reverse order: for (int i = rhsLen-1; i>=0; i--) stack[top++] = table[rhsStart + i]. No stackalloc, no copy.
perf.rationale: Removes a stackalloc-in-loop (potential unbounded frame growth and stack overflow) and an O(rhsLen) copy pass per expansion. Burst/JIT will not hoist a loop-body stackalloc, so this is a real frame-size and cycle win.
perf.risk: None — table[rhsStart+i] is read in the same reverse order the copy produced; observable behavior identical. Strictly safer.

perf.summary: AggressiveInlining on a method containing stackalloc and an unbounded parse loop is unlikely to help and may bloat callers.
perf.currentCost: [MethodImpl(AggressiveInlining)] on a large method with stackalloc; inlining a stackalloc into the caller can enlarge the caller frame and is often ignored by the JIT/Burst for big bodies.
perf.proposedChange: Drop AggressiveInlining here (keep it on genuine hot leaf methods like SuffixOracle.Contains). After removing the in-loop stackalloc, the remaining stackalloc[len*2+2] is the only frame allocation.
perf.rationale: Avoids code-size bloat at call sites and misleading intent; inlining a top-level parser entry point rarely pays off. Keeps Burst codegen focused.
perf.risk: Purely an attribute change; no semantic effect. Verify no caller relied on inlining for a measured win (none expected for an entry point).
